caps.text: Anthropic replaced Git.
Not because Git is bad. Because AI writes code too fast.
In May 2026, they merged about 2,500 changes a day.
By September, over 30,000 a day.
A team of seven built a new system from scratch in five months.
Why switch? What did they build? And what did they learn?
First: how big is their monorepo?
The main branch's history: almost 100 GB. One compressed working copy: over 25 GB.
CI alone checks out the code about 25 million times a day,
not counting dev environments, agent sandboxes and research jobs.
Fetched naively, that would be over 600 petabytes a day.
Git has tools for this: shallow clones, sparse checkouts, promisor remotes.
They used them all, and at the peak ran several hundred git mirrors.
But the faster they merged, the further their snapshots fell behind,
and keeping diff and blame working on partial clones took more and more care.
Then they stepped back and noticed something.
Git is distributed: every clone is a complete repository that works fully offline.
But like most companies, they were using it as a centralized system.
And nearly all of their clients were agents and jobs: online by definition.
The very things that make Git great offline were holding them back.
So they asked: what if source control assumed, from day one, that clients are always online?
The answer is called Scion.
One: clients are always online, and fetch data only when they need it.
Two: the server does the heavy lifting. History, blame, commits, merges, rebases.
Three: every query is an API, so many jobs need no local repo at all.
Four: everything scales out. No full copy of the repo exists anywhere, not even on the server.
Five: commits are cheap, incremental and lock-free. Their cost scales with the change, not the repo.
Six: the working copy is optional. When you do need files, you only pay for what you read.
How does it work? In Scion, the unit of work is a changeset.
A git commit points to a whole tree.
A changeset lists only the files that changed, and where their contents live.
It's created on the server. No packfiles, no locks, and it's available everywhere instantly.
Blame and file history come from “derived data”, computed from each changeset’s parents,
computed only when needed, and improved anytime without the client knowing.
Fetching flips too: the client never says what it has. Only what it wants.
Every object is immutable, so any cache can answer.
Three tiers: a daemon on every machine, a cache in every region, and finally the server.
Every tier keeps a cache hit rate above 99 percent,
and the tiers are strictly isolated, so one failure cannot take down the whole system.
The result? 200 times less CPU and memory than the old git mirrors.
Checkouts for CI and research went from minutes to seconds.
CI alone got back 25 percent of its CPU.
The most surprising part is how few people built it.
Seven people built Scion, Antique, their code review tool, and half a dozen related systems,
and fully migrated in five months, while daily merges grew tenfold.
One detail: they had hand-written an ingestion pipeline, and thought it was good.
They gave it to an early internal snapshot of a new model, with no further instructions.
It used 20 times less memory, ran 4 times faster, and kept every implicit invariant.
Every engineer on the team now rates Claude as a better coder than themselves.
So what do people do? Understand the system, make the tradeoffs, and very often, tell Claude "no."
Like piling extra validation onto a trusted internal service over a hypothetical risk. No.
Reviews moved from reading every line to checking intent.
They also gave every component a Claude "superfan":
it watches telemetry and logs all day, and spots subtle issues that alerts miss.
Even merge queues: while tests run, hundreds or thousands of changes can land.
So there is no global lock. They test after merge and before deploy,
and when changes conflict, Claude usually fixes them faster than humans can spot them.
So should everyone ditch Git? No.
They say Scion only makes sense for enormous monorepos. It is not a general replacement for Git.
But they expect this class of problem to become common in the next six to twelve months.
So they want to bring the ideas back to Git: richer server-side APIs, sparse and shallow features that compose,
working with GitHub, GitLab and the open-source community.
Writing code isn't the bottleneck anymore.
It moved to every tool built for human speed.
So what breaks next?
